items.q: Match the following insulin features — 1) Chain length 2) Receptor type 3) Receptor kinase 4) Pre-prohormone … A) 51 amino acids in two chains B) Tyrosine kinase receptor C) Insulin receptor substrate (IRS) D) Preproinsulin
items.exp: Insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains; receptor is a tyrosine kinase; downstream signalling uses IRS proteins; the precursor is preproinsulin. (Book p927)

items.q: A neonate has refractory hyperglycaemia with severe insulin resistance and elevated triglycerides. The most likely genetic defect involves the:
items.exp: Severe insulin resistance with hyperglycaemia in a neonate is consistent with insulin-receptor mutations (Donohue or Rabson-Mendenhall). (Book p927)

items.q: Assess insulin structure: I Insulin is composed of A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges. II C-peptide remains attached in mature insulin.
items.exp: Insulin has A and B chains linked by disulphide bonds; C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin and is not part of mature insulin. (Book p927)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a step in insulin biosynthesis?
items.exp: Insulin does not directly produce glucose; it lowers glucose by promoting uptake and inhibiting production. (Book p927)

items.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose primarily by stimulating glucose uptake via ___ translocation.
items.exp: GLUT4 translocation to the muscle and adipocyte membrane is insulin's main glucose-lowering step. (Book p927)

items.q: Match the following stimulus — 1) Glucose 2) Amino acids (especially leucine) 3) Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) 4) Vagal stimulation … A) Most potent stimulus for insulin secretion B) Stimulus during protein-rich meals C) Augment glucose-stimulated secretion D) Cephalic-phase insulin release
items.exp: Glucose is the most potent stimulus; amino acids (especially leucine) trigger protein-meal insulin; incretins augment glucose-stimulated secretion; vagal activity drives cephalic-phase release. (Book p927)

items.q: A patient has postprandial hypoglycaemia after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. The most consistent mechanism is:
items.exp: Roux-en-Y bypass causes rapid glucose delivery with exaggerated GLP-1 and insulin surges, producing late hypoglycaemia. (Book p927)

items.q: Assess insulin secretion phases: I First phase peaks within minutes and lasts ~10 minutes. II Second phase is sustained and involves newly synthesised insulin.
items.exp: First phase releases stored granules within minutes; second phase is sustained and involves newly synthesised insulin. (Book p927)

items.q: Match the following ion channel / enzyme — 1) K-ATP channel 2) Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel 3) KIR6.2 subunit 4) SUR1 subunit … A) Closes on ATP rise B) Opens to trigger exocytosis C) Forms pore of K-ATP D) Sulfonylurea receptor
items.exp: ATP closes K-ATP channels; depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels triggering exocytosis; KIR6.2 forms the pore and SUR1 binds sulfonylureas. (Book p927)

items.q: A patient uses sulfonylurea and experiences hypoglycaemia. The mechanism is most consistent with:
opts: Closure of K-ATP channels on β-cells
items.exp: Sulfonylureas bind SUR1, closing K-ATP channels, depolarising the β-cell and triggering insulin release. (Book p927)

items.q: Insulin receptor signalling involves phosphorylation of ___ proteins.
items.exp: IRS proteins are phosphorylated by the insulin-receptor tyrosine kinase, activating PI3K and downstream metabolic effects. (Book p927)

items.q: Assess insulin effects: I Insulin suppresses lipolysis in adipocytes. II Insulin stimulates glycogenolysis in liver.
items.exp: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and gluconeogenesis; it stimulates glycogen synthesis, not glycogenolysis. (Book p927)
